newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Christopher says U.S. won't abandon Africa.
newsitem.headline: Christopher says U.S. won't abandon Africa.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Saturday defended the role of the United States in Africa, saying it would not "walk away".
But Christopher, on his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa since taking office in 1993, conceded that there was debate over how important the region was for the United States.

"I will not pretend to you that there is no debate in America about Africa's relative importance...(but) we cannot and will not walk away," he said in a speech at Witwatersrand University, in which he indirectly accused France of trying to maintain exclusive patronage in the region.
Christopher encountered some hurdles on Saturday to U.S. ideas for region.

South African President Nelson Mandela responded coolly to his proposed African crisis intervention force and Angola's former rebels said their leader would not meet Christopher when he visits the country for talks on the peace process on Monday.

Africa needed "the support of all its many friends, not the exclusive patronage of a few", Christopher said in unusually strong comments aimed at France. Officials in Paris were quoted in news reports this week as criticising his visit, which takes place just a few weeks before the U.S. presidential elections.
"All nations must cooperate, not compete, if we are going to make a positive difference in Africa's future," he said.
Aides were clearly miffed by the broadside from Paris.
"The French are upset because they consider Africa to be their private domain. They feel threatened if others also want to make a contribution," said one official.

Christopher has been promoting U.S. plans for an all-Africa force that could be deployed in times of crisis, but Mandela, whose support is seen as vital, said he would only throw his weight behind it if it was set up through the United Nations.
"My point of view is if this initiative is to succeed, it must have credibility. It (the initiative) must not come from one country," Mandela said after meeting Christopher in Cape Town.
"It should be the initiative of the United Nations. In such a case it would receive wide support," he told reporters.
Christopher has also been encouraging African leaders to propose candidates to replace U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose reappointment Washington has vowed to veto.
But Mandela said African states supported Boutros-Ghali in his quest for another term, despite U.S. opposition.

Boutros-Ghali, the first secretary-general from the African continent, ends his five years in office on December 31 and the United States is trying to persuade members to dump him for failing to give enough attention to restructuring the body.
Christopher, who returned to Cape Town on Saturday evening after Johannesburg speech, is to go to Angola on Monday on the last leg of his five-nation tour.

There he is expected to meet President Jose Eduardo dos Santos, but the UNITA former rebel movement said its leader Jonas Savimbi would not meet Christopher for talks on the shaky peace process that ended nearly 20 years of civil war.

"I want to make it clear that Dr Savimbi will not come to Luanda to meet Warren Christopher. Political conditions are not favourable to allow this to happen," UNITA spokesman Isias Samukuva said. Savimbi has several times refused to go to the capital from his stronghold in the north of the country.
In his speech Christopher said the United States had been deeply engaged in peace efforts in Angola and Mozambique, among many other involvements in the continent.

The Clinton administration had sought to protect aid to Africa, gave $600 million towards South Africa's transition from apartheid and helped to consolidate democracy in Mali and Benin -- two former French colonies.
Also, U.S. troops provided critical support for relief efforts in Rwanda and saved hundreds of thousands of lives in Somalia, he added.
